items.title: Late tram
items.body:
Half the seats are sleeping,
the other half are me.
The city passes softly,
lit like a slow sea.

I do not need to be anywhere
faster than this light.
The stops say their own names aloud
and hand me to the night.

items.title: Consistent hashing in one breath
items.body: With plain hash(key) mod N, adding one server reshuffles almost every key. Consistent hashing places both servers and keys on a ring and assigns each key to the next server clockwise. Add or remove a server and only about 1/N of the keys move. Virtual nodes (many points per server) smooth out the load.
items.q: Roughly what fraction of keys move when you add a server under consistent hashing?
items.a: About 1/N, versus nearly all keys with plain mod-N hashing.

items.title: Total Chess pilot opens in Budapest on 10 November
items.body: Norway Chess's FIDE-approved Total Chess event runs from 10 to 20 November at the Anantara New York Palace in Budapest. It combines three time controls: Fast Classic (45 minutes + 30 seconds), rapid and blitz. Twenty-four players, including Carlsen, Caruana, Praggnanandhaa, Arjun Erigaisi and Vaishali Rameshbabu, start with a blitz Swiss, then groups and knockouts. It pilots a full tour starting in March 2027.

items.title: Enter late, leave early
items.body: A screenwriting rule that works for any story: start a scene as late as possible and leave as soon as its point has landed. Skip the hellos and the walking in; open on the moment something shifts. Readers fill in the rest, and they enjoy doing it.
items.hook: Wonder: which sentence in your last piece is the real first sentence?

items.title: Olympus Mons, the gentle giant
items.body: Olympus Mons on Mars is the tallest volcano known in the solar system, rising about 22 km above its surroundings, roughly two and a half times Everest's height above sea level. Its slopes are so gentle that someone standing on it would barely notice the climb, and the summit would sit beyond the horizon.
items.q: Roughly how tall is Olympus Mons?
items.a: About 22 km, around 2.5 times Everest's height above sea level.

items.body: To speak harsh words when sweet ones are at hand is like plucking unripe fruit when the ripe is there for the taking.

items.title: The Mother of All Demos
items.body: On 9 December 1968 in San Francisco, Douglas Engelbart and his team showed the world a computer mouse, hypertext links, windowed views, collaborative real-time editing and video conferencing, all in one 90-minute presentation. Much of modern computing was previewed in that single afternoon.
items.q: Who gave the 1968 'Mother of All Demos' that introduced the mouse?
items.a: Douglas Engelbart.

items.title: Make the first step embarrassingly small
items.body: If a task won't start, shrink the first step until it feels almost silly: open the file; put on one shoe; write a single sentence. Starting is the bottleneck, and momentum usually does the rest. If it doesn't, that's fine too: you still moved, and that counts.

items.title: Wombats make cube-shaped droppings
items.body: Wombats are the only animals known to produce cube-shaped poo. A 2018 study found that the final stretch of their intestine has walls with varying stiffness that shape the droppings into cubes. Wombats stack them on rocks and logs as territorial markers, and the flat sides help them stay put.
items.hook: Wonder: what other shapes could nature 'manufacture' without any moulds?

items.title: Context compaction, the agent's tidy desk
items.body: Long-running agents fill their context window with old tool outputs and chatter. Compaction replaces older turns with a short summary while keeping recent turns verbatim. It's a trade: you keep the thread of the work and free space, but anything the summary leaves out is gone. Good compaction keeps decisions, open questions and file paths; it drops raw logs.
items.hook: Wonder: if you summarised your own workday in five lines, what would you be sure to keep?

items.title: Nalanda, the great monastery-university
items.body: Nalanda in present-day Bihar grew into a famous centre of learning from about the 5th century CE, under Gupta patronage. Students came from across Asia; the Chinese pilgrim-scholar Xuanzang studied there in the 7th century and wrote about its scholars and libraries. Its ruins are now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
items.q: Which Chinese scholar studied at Nalanda in the 7th century?
items.a: Xuanzang.

items.title: The generation effect
items.body: You remember information better when you produce it yourself than when you simply read it. Slamecka and Graf described this in 1978: completing 'hot: c___' (cold) sticks better than reading 'hot: cold'. A cheap way to use it: before re-reading notes, try to write the key point from memory first.
items.hook: Wonder: what could you try to recall right now, before looking it up?

items.title: Java records: data, said plainly
items.body: Records, final since Java 16 (JEP 395), are a compact way to declare a class that is just data: record Point(int x, int y) {}. The compiler supplies the constructor, accessors x() and y(), equals, hashCode and toString. Fields are final, so records are shallowly immutable, which makes them ideal for DTOs, map keys and values passed between threads.
items.q: Which methods does the compiler generate for a Java record?
items.a: A canonical constructor, accessor methods, equals, hashCode and toString.

items.title: The opposition, in one picture
items.body: In king-and-pawn endings, two kings standing on the same file with one empty square between them are 'in opposition'. Whoever is NOT to move holds the opposition, because the other king must step aside and give ground. Many 'drawn or won?' pawn endings come down to this tiny standoff.
items.q: With kings facing each other one square apart, who has the opposition?
items.a: The side that is not to move.

items.title: The lending library of umbrellas
items.body: The bus stop had a bucket of umbrellas and a sign: Take one. Bring one back. Nobody knew who started it. Mira took a yellow one in June and forgot it for months. In October she returned it with a second umbrella, blue, that she'd bought on purpose. The next morning both were gone, and someone had left a third: green, with a note tied to the handle that said only, 'Your turn was lovely.'

items.title: Agents get their own identities in HashiCorp Vault
items.body: At IBM TechXchange on 27 October, IBM made HashiCorp Vault 2.2 with Agent Identity generally available, and previewed a new Secure Hub. The idea: each AI agent gets its own managed identity and short-lived credentials, rather than borrowing a human's keys. Integrations named include watsonx Orchestrate, Amazon Bedrock, Microsoft Foundry and Google Gemini.

items.title: Sharks are older than trees
items.body: Sharks appear in the fossil record around 450 million years ago. The earliest true trees came later, roughly 385 to 390 million years ago. So sharks were already swimming the seas before there were any forests on land.
items.q: Which came first, sharks or trees?
items.a: Sharks, by roughly 60 million years.

items.title: Hubble and Webb read the solar system's oldest postcards
items.body: Astronomers used Hubble and Webb together to study 27 small, distant objects beyond Neptune. These icy bodies have changed little since the solar system formed, so their surfaces act like a preserved record of the material the planets were built from.
items.hook: Wonder: what would a 4.5-billion-year-old snowball tell you about the day it formed?

items.title: Grace Hopper's nanosecond
items.body: To explain why satellite signals and fast computers were limited by distance, Grace Hopper handed out pieces of wire about 30 cm (11.8 inches) long: the distance light travels in one billionth of a second. She'd sometimes contrast it with a coil of wire representing a microsecond, nearly 300 metres long.
items.hook: Wonder: how far does light travel in the time your laptop finishes one clock cycle?

items.title: Interleaving: mix the practice
items.body: Practising one problem type in a block feels smooth, but mixing types (A, C, B, A, B, C) tends to produce better long-term results. Studies on maths learning, such as Rohrer and Taylor's, found that interleaved practice helps you learn to tell which method a problem needs, not just how to run the method. It feels harder while you do it, which is part of why it works.
items.q: Why does interleaved practice often beat blocked practice?
items.a: It trains you to recognise which strategy a problem needs, not just to execute one strategy repeatedly.

items.body: Nothing, Lucilius, is ours, except time.
items.who: Seneca, Letters to Lucilius, Letter I (tr. Gummere)

items.title: Leave a breadcrumb before you stop
items.body: Before you step away from a task, write one line: the very next physical action. Not 'finish the report', but 'open the draft and rewrite the second heading'. Restarting is often the hardest part with ADHD; a breadcrumb means future-you doesn't have to rebuild the whole mental map before taking the first step.

items.title: 1,330 couplets, built like a grid
items.body: Thiruvalluvar's Thirukkural is precisely structured: 133 chapters of 10 couplets each, 1,330 kurals in all. It is divided into three books: Aram (virtue), Porul (wealth and statecraft) and Inbam (love). Each kural is a two-line venba of seven metrical feet, four in the first line and three in the second.
items.q: How many chapters and couplets does the Thirukkural have?
items.a: 133 chapters of 10 couplets: 1,330 kurals, in three books (Aram, Porul, Inbam).

items.title: Backpressure: letting the slow part say 'not yet'
items.body: When a producer is faster than a consumer, something has to give. Without backpressure, queues grow until memory runs out. With it, the consumer signals how much it can take, and the producer slows down. Bounded queues that block, TCP's flow-control window, and Reactive Streams' request(n) are all the same idea: demand flows upstream, data flows downstream.
items.hook: Wonder: where in your system is an unbounded queue quietly waiting to become a memory problem?

items.title: Kettle
items.body:
The kettle hums its one long vowel,
the window fogs, then clears.
Nothing in this kitchen asks
for more than what is here.

Steam climbs and quietly forgets
the water it once was.
I pour, and let the evening be
exactly what it does.

items.title: Nihal Sarin enters the world top 20
items.body: The November FIDE list has Nihal Sarin at 2720, up 11 points and climbing from #30 to #19, a career-best ranking. It follows a 5/6 score and a board-two gold medal at the European Club Cup in Budva. At the top, Magnus Carlsen is on 2823, and Javokhir Sindarov sits at #4 with 2782.
items.q: What is Nihal Sarin's world ranking on the November 2026 FIDE list?
items.a: #19, rated 2720: his career best.

items.title: Southern Taurids peak this Thursday
items.body: The Southern Taurid meteor shower peaks in the early hours of 5 November. Expect a gentle 5 to 10 meteors an hour, but Taurids are slow and sometimes bright: the occasional fireball is their signature. The debris comes from Comet Encke. The Northern Taurids follow, peaking closer to 12 November, just after the 9 November new Moon gives a dark sky.
items.q: Which comet feeds the Taurid meteor showers?
items.a: Comet 2P/Encke.

items.title: OpenAI ships GPT-6.1 Terra for workflow agents
items.body: OpenAI rolled out GPT-6.1 Terra on 26 October, a mid-tier model aimed at computer use and workflow automation. It is available in ChatGPT Work, Codex and the API, and is priced at half of the GPT-5.6 Terra model it replaces. On OpenAI's own internal stress test, its error rate fell from 53.6% to 16.7% at low reasoning effort, and to 4.3% at maximum effort.
items.hook: Wonder: for your own agent tasks, would you rather pay for more 'thinking' per step, or for more steps?

items.title: Quick retrieval: this edition
items.body:
Close your eyes for 30 seconds and recall three things from today's feed without scrolling back. Then check.

Pulling memories out, rather than re-reading them, is how they stick.
items.q: Little's Law in one line?
items.a: Items in the system = arrival rate × time in system (L = λW).

items.body: There is nothing either good or bad, but thinking makes it so.

items.title: Older than the Aztecs
items.body: Teaching was happening at Oxford by 1096. The Aztec capital Tenochtitlan was founded in 1325, more than two centuries later.
items.hook: Which institutions around you will still exist in 900 years?

items.title: The first published program
items.body: In 1843 Ada Lovelace translated an article about Babbage's Analytical Engine and added notes three times longer than the original. Note G laid out step by step how the engine could compute Bernoulli numbers. It's often called the first published computer program, written for a machine that was never built.
items.hook: What would it feel like to write code for a machine that doesn't exist yet?

items.title: Park downhill
items.body:
Hemingway liked to stop writing while he still knew what came next, so the next morning's start was easy.

For ADHD this is gold. End every work block by writing one sentence: "Next, I will…". Starting is the hardest part; leave yourself a downhill start.
items.hook: What's the one-line 'next' for the task you'll open after this?

items.title: Two lamps
items.body:
Two lamps hung in a temple corridor. One burned bright and needed refilling twice a night. The other burned low and lasted till dawn.

The priest never compared them. He knew some hours need brightness and some need endurance, and a corridor needs both.

items.title: CAP, said properly
items.body:
CAP is often summarised as 'pick two of three.' More precisely: when a network partition happens, a distributed system must choose between consistency (refuse or delay answers) and availability (answer, possibly with stale data). When there's no partition, you can have both.

Brewer stated it in 2000; Gilbert and Lynch proved it in 2002.
items.q: When is CAP's trade-off forced?
items.a: Only during a network partition. Then you choose consistency or availability.

items.body: Learn thoroughly what is worth learning, then stand by it in how you live.

items.title: Aryabhata's spinning Earth
items.body: In 499 CE, at just 23, Aryabhata wrote the Aryabhatiya. He proposed that the stars' daily motion comes from Earth rotating on its axis, and gave a value of π accurate to four decimal places (3.1416). India's first satellite was named after him in 1975.
items.q: What did Aryabhata say explains the stars' daily motion?
items.a: Earth's rotation on its own axis.

items.title: Context isn't memory
items.body:
A model's context window is like a desk: whatever is on it right now, it can use. Memory is the filing cabinet: what you choose to pull back onto the desk later.

RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) is just a librarian who fetches the right files before each question. Most 'the AI forgot' problems are really retrieval problems.
items.hook: In your own systems, where is the right information sitting in a cabinet nobody opens?

items.title: Bananas are berries; strawberries aren't
items.body: Botanically, a berry develops from a single flower's ovary with seeds inside the flesh, so bananas, tomatoes and even brinjal qualify. A strawberry's 'seeds' are actually tiny fruits on the outside of a swollen stem base, so it isn't a true berry at all.

items.title: The Y2038 problem
items.body: Unix counts time as seconds since 1 January 1970. In a signed 32-bit integer, that counter overflows at 03:14:07 UTC on 19 January 2038 and wraps around to 1901. Most modern systems use 64 bits now, but old embedded devices and file formats may still break.
items.hook: What 32-bit assumptions are lurking in systems you've worked on?

items.title: Building a bridge (the Lucena position)
items.body:
Rook and pawn vs rook, your pawn on the 7th, your king on the queening square, enemy rook cutting your king off from the side. How do you get out and promote?

The classic method: bring your rook to the 4th rank, walk the king out, and when checks come, block with the rook. That's 'building a bridge.'
items.q: In the Lucena position, which rank does the rook go to, and why?
items.a: The 4th rank, counting from your side. That way it can step in front of your king to block the checks once the king leaves the pawn.

items.title: The inverted U
items.body:
In 1908 Yerkes and Dodson found that performance rises with arousal, but only up to a point. Then it falls. The peak sits lower for complex tasks than simple ones.

Translation: a little pressure sharpens you for routine work; for deep, tricky work (debugging, writing), calm wins.
items.hook: Is the stress you feel today helping simple tasks or hurting complex ones?

items.title: Late-November sky diary
items.body: Mark these: Nov 16, Mars passes close to Jupiter. Nov 24, the full Moon is a supermoon. Nov 25, Uranus reaches opposition, its closest and brightest of the year (still needs binoculars and a dark sky).

items.title: What the river knows
items.body:
It never argues with the stone.
It simply goes around,
and in a thousand years
the stone is sand,
and the river
is still a river.

items.title: Java 21 virtual threads, in one breath
items.body:
Platform threads map one-to-one onto OS threads and are expensive, so you pool them. Virtual threads (final in Java 21) are cheap threads managed by the JVM. When one blocks on I/O, the JVM parks it and frees the carrier thread.

Result: you can write simple blocking code and still handle a million concurrent requests.
items.q: What happens to a virtual thread when it blocks on I/O?
items.a: The JVM unmounts it from its carrier OS thread, which is freed to run another virtual thread.

items.title: Zero gets its rules
items.body: In 628 CE the mathematician Brahmagupta, in his Brahmasphutasiddhanta, wrote the first known rules for doing arithmetic with zero as a number in its own right: a number minus itself is zero, anything times zero is zero. He also wrestled with division by zero, a problem that still trips up our code.
items.q: Who first wrote down arithmetic rules for zero, and when?
items.a: Brahmagupta, in 628 CE.

items.body: Men are disturbed not by things, but by the principles and notions which they form concerning things.

items.title: Body doubling
items.body:
Some tasks get done simply because someone else is in the room. That's body doubling. The other person doesn't help; their presence just anchors your attention.

Works remotely too: a silent video call with a friend, or a 'focus room' online. Even saying "I'm starting X now" to someone counts.
items.hook: Who could be your silent co-worker for one hour this week?

items.title: The first programmers of ENIAC
items.body: ENIAC, unveiled in 1946, was programmed by six women: Kay McNulty, Betty Jennings, Betty Snyder, Marlyn Wescoff, Fran Bilas and Ruth Lichterman. There were no programming languages; they worked from wiring diagrams and plugged cables by hand. For decades they went largely uncredited.

items.title: Three hearts, blue blood
items.body: An octopus has three hearts: two pump blood through the gills, one pumps it around the body. Its blood is blue because it carries oxygen with copper-based haemocyanin instead of our iron-based haemoglobin.
items.hook: Why would copper beat iron in cold, low-oxygen seawater?

items.title: The Zeigarnik effect, honestly
items.body:
In the 1920s Bluma Zeigarnik noticed that waiters remembered unpaid orders perfectly and forgot them once paid. Her experiments suggested unfinished tasks stay mentally 'open.'

Later replications are mixed, but one useful finding holds: writing down a concrete plan for an unfinished task quiets the mental nagging. Closing the loop on paper is enough.
items.hook: What open loop is humming in your head right now? Write the next step down.

items.title: A teaspoon of neutron star
items.body: A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a ball about 20 km wide, roughly the size of a city. A teaspoon of its material would weigh on the order of a billion tonnes on Earth.
items.q: Roughly how wide is a neutron star?
items.a: About 20 km, city-sized, while holding more mass than the Sun.

items.title: More games than atoms
items.body: Claude Shannon estimated the number of possible chess games at about 10^120, now called the Shannon number. The observable universe has roughly 10^80 atoms. No computer will ever solve chess by brute force, which is why intuition and pattern still matter.
items.hook: If brute force is impossible, how do engines play so well?

items.title: Evals are the unit tests of AI
items.body:
You wouldn't ship code without tests, but people ship prompts without evals all the time. An eval is a fixed set of inputs with known good outputs that you re-run after every change.

Start tiny: 10 real examples, a pass/fail column. It turns 'feels better' into 'is better.'

items.title: The three-beat story
items.body:
Every story that holds a room has three beats: someone wants something → something gets in the way → they (or we) change.

No change, no story; just an event. Before your next speech or blog post, write one line: "Who changed, and how?"
items.hook: What's the smallest true story from your week that has all three beats?

items.title: Idempotency keys: making 'retry' safe
items.body:
A payment request times out. Did it go through? If the client retries, you might charge twice.

The fix: the client sends a unique idempotency key with the request. The server stores the result against that key, so a repeat with the same key returns the stored result instead of doing the work again. Stripe made the pattern famous; every order and payment API needs it.
items.q: What does the server do when it sees an idempotency key it has seen before?
items.a: Returns the stored response from the first attempt without re-executing the operation.

items.title: The temple whose shadow stories are wrong
items.body: Rajaraja Chola I completed the Brihadeeswarar temple at Thanjavur around 1010 CE. Its tower rises about 66 metres. A popular legend says the tower casts no shadow at noon. It does cast one; it just falls on its own broad base. The real wonder is that it has stood for over a thousand years.
items.hook: Why do we love myths about things that are already remarkable?

items.body: There are more things, Lucilius, likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality.

items.title: Make time visible
items.body: Time blindness is real: an ADHD brain often feels only 'now' and 'not now.' Move time outside your head. Use a visual countdown timer on the desk, or say out loud "this gets 25 minutes." Analog clocks help more than digital ones, because you can see how much of the hour is left.
items.hook: Where in your day does time disappear the most?

items.title: Java was almost called Oak
items.body: In 1991 James Gosling's team at Sun started the 'Green Project' to program consumer devices. Their language was called Oak, after a tree outside his office. A trademark clash forced a new name, and in 1995 it shipped as Java, sold on 'write once, run anywhere.'
items.q: What was Java's original name, and why did it change?
items.a: Oak. The name was already trademarked, so it was renamed Java before the 1995 launch.

items.title: Cleopatra and the Moon landing
items.body: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Apollo 11 Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza. The pyramid went up around 2560 BCE; she died in 30 BCE. That's about 2,530 years before her and 1,999 years after.
items.hook: What else feels ancient but is actually 'recent'?

items.title: The physiological sigh
items.body:
Two inhales through the nose (a full one, then a short top-up) and one long, slow exhale through the mouth. A 2023 Stanford study found that five minutes a day of this 'cyclic sighing' lifted mood more than the same time spent on mindfulness meditation.

It's the fastest manual brake on stress your body offers.

source.name: Balban et al., Cell Reports Medicine (2023)

items.title: Capablanca's unusual advice: learn endings first
items.body: José Raúl Capablanca, world champion 1921–27, told beginners to study the endgame before anything else. With few pieces on the board, you learn what each piece is actually worth. Openings are memory. Endgames are understanding.
items.hook: What's the 'endgame' of your own field: the simplest situation where the fundamentals show clearly?

items.title: Leonids peak Nov 17–18
items.body: The Leonid meteor shower peaks on the night of 17–18 November, at around 15 meteors an hour under dark skies. The Moon will have set by the second half of the night. Leonids are among the fastest meteors, hitting the air at about 70 km/s. They're dust from Comet Tempel–Tuttle.
items.hook: A grain of sand making a streak across the whole sky. How much energy is that?

items.title: Java: when a HashMap bucket turns into a tree
items.body: Since Java 8, if one HashMap bucket collects more than 8 entries (and the table has at least 64 slots), that bucket turns from a linked list into a red-black tree. Worst-case lookup drops from O(n) to O(log n). It's a defence against bad hashCode() methods and hash-flooding attacks.
items.q: Two conditions trigger treeification. What are they?
items.a: More than 8 entries in one bucket (TREEIFY_THRESHOLD) and a table capacity of at least 64. Below 64 slots, HashMap resizes instead.

items.title: The clockmaker's apprentice
items.body:
The apprentice asked why the old man oiled clocks that were running perfectly.

"Because," he said, "the day it stops, you'll be busy with a hundred others. A clock doesn't ask for care when it needs it. It asks a month later, all at once."

The boy thought this was about clocks. Thirty years later, oiling a quiet clock in his own shop, he realised it never had been.

items.title: An agent is just a loop
items.body:
Strip the hype and every AI agent is: observe → decide → act → check → repeat.

Most agent failures aren't bad thinking. They're a bad 'check' step: the agent never verifies its action worked, so errors compound silently. If you build agents, spend your effort on the check.
items.hook: In your own work, where is the 'check' step weakest?

items.title: A day on Venus outlasts its year
items.body: Venus turns on its axis once every 243 Earth days but goes around the Sun in about 225. It also spins backwards compared with most planets, so on Venus the Sun would rise in the west.
items.hook: What could have knocked a whole planet into spinning backwards?

items.title: Forgetting is the point
items.body:
In 1885 Hermann Ebbinghaus memorised nonsense syllables and tracked how fast he lost them. Recall fell steeply within the first day, then flattened.

The twist: each time you pull a memory back just as it's fading, it decays more slowly afterwards. That's the spacing effect. Struggling a little to remember is the signal that learning is happening.
items.q: When is the best time to review something?
items.a: Just as you're about to forget it, so retrieval takes some effort. Then space the next review further out.

items.title: The first actual bug
items.body: On 9 September 1947, operators of the Harvard Mark II found a moth trapped in a relay. They taped it into the logbook with the note "First actual case of bug being found." Grace Hopper loved telling the story. Engineers had already been using "bug" for faults, so the joke was that this one was literal.
items.q: What machine was the famous moth found in?
items.a: The Harvard Mark II, in 1947.

items.body: Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits.
items.hook: What would today look like if you judged it only by effort given?

items.title: A dam that has worked for nearly 2,000 years
items.body: The Kallanai, or Grand Anicut, on the Kaveri is credited to the Chola king Karikalan, around the 2nd century CE. It's among the oldest water-diversion structures in the world still in use, and it still feeds irrigation channels in the delta today.
items.hook: What makes a structure last 2,000 years when most concrete gives out in 100?

items.title: Interest is your ignition, not importance
items.body:
Many ADHD coaches describe attention as running on interest rather than importance. The usual starters go by the acronym INCUP: Interest, Novelty, Challenge, Urgency, Passion.

When a task won't start, don't ask "why can't I make myself?" Ask which of the five you can add. Make it a race against a timer (challenge, urgency), try a new tool (novelty), or attach it to a question you care about (interest).
items.hook: Which of the five is cheapest to add to your next boring task?

items.title: Gukesh vs Sindarov: the world title match is three weeks away
items.body: The 2026 World Championship match runs in Geneva from November 25 to December 15, with reigning champion Gukesh D defending against Javokhir Sindarov of Uzbekistan. Both players are about 20, making it the youngest pairing ever to contest the title.
items.hook: What changes in a 14-game match that doesn't exist in a tournament?

items.title: Cab window, 10 pm
items.body:
The city folds its noise away
like laundry into drawers.
One lit window, then another —
someone else's evening, not yours,
and somehow that is restful:
to pass a hundred lives
and owe none of them a reply.

items.title: Little's Law: the formula hiding inside every queue
items.body:
L = λ × W. Items in the system = arrival rate × average time each one stays.

If 10 incidents arrive a day and each takes 3 days to close, you'll average about 30 open. The law doesn't care who works harder. To shrink the queue you can only reduce arrivals or reduce time-in-system.
items.hook: Which lever is easier in your queue: fewer arrivals, or less time per item?
items.q: Arrival rate doubles, time-per-item stays the same. What happens to the open queue?
items.a: It doubles. L = λW is linear in both.

items.title: Mistral opens up a trillion-parameter model
items.body: Mistral released Large 4 with open weights: a trillion-parameter multimodal model that organisations can run on their own servers. It's pitched at software development and defensive security work, where companies don't want sensitive data leaving their walls.
items.hook: If the weights are free, what are companies actually paying for?

items.title: Before dawn: the Moon visits Mars and Jupiter
items.body: Over the next couple of mornings a thin waning Moon slides past Mars and Jupiter, then Regulus, the heart of Leo. Look east in the hour before sunrise. Jupiter is the steady bright one; Mars is fainter and faintly orange.
items.q: Why do stars twinkle but planets mostly don't?
items.a: Stars are so far away they're effectively single points, so air turbulence bends that one point around. A planet shows a tiny disc, and the wobbles from different parts of the disc average out.
